newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Hong Kong shares hit fresh high, Tokyo ends lower.
newsitem.headline: Hong Kong shares hit fresh high, Tokyo ends lower.

text.p: Hong Kong's Hang Seng index capped a record-breaking week with its third consecutive all-time closing high on Friday.
The index rose 25.72 points, or 0.19 percent, to close at 13,856.40, after reaching a session high of 13,977.54 with gains in banking offsetting profit-taking in property counters.
"In general, market sentiment is still quite bullish," said Frederick Tsang, head of research at PrimeEast Securities.
"I think entering 1997, we sense that more foreigners want to buy shares in Hong Kong." he said.
Elsewhere in Asia, markets were mixed.
Tokyo shares closed lower as early gains, mainly prompted by buying back in the construction sector, lost momentum.

The Nikkei 225 average, which rose over 300 points early in the afternoon, ended down 54.30 points or 0.30 percent at 18,090.04. The stock market had plunged by more than 2,000 points in the first trading week of this year.
In Singapore, a surge of foreign funds late in the session boosted an otherwise sedate stock market, dealers said.
An inflow of funds from the United States and Britain resulted in a flurry of activity as volumes rose to more than 327 million shares -- a daily level unseen for over a year.
"About US$100 million from the U.S. were channelled through two U.S. houses to be pumped into various blue chips in Singapore," said a dealer with one of the U.S. houses.
The benchmark Straits Times Industrials Index ended 23.85 points, or 1.07 percent, up at 2,244.21.
In Sydney, a dull Australian share market ambled to a flat finish, with big banks bolstering a soft industrial sector, and mining stocks saw recent gains cut as base metals prices fell.
The All Ordinaries index lost just 0.8 points to 2,435.5.
Stocks closed sharply lower in Seoul on widespread profit-taking after rising over the past week, brokers said.
The composite index ended at a provisional 701.18, down 1.5 percent or 10.68 points, after touching an intra-day low of 695.77 and a high of 720.41.

The market has risen by more than 16 percent since the middle of last week, at first on the back of speculation that mergers and acquisitions would become active among banks and then due to expectations of increasing foreign buying.
The current wave of strikes, which started late last year in protest against a new labour law, has already been fully discounted, brokers said.
In Thailand, stocks closed higher on foreign bargain hunting for discounted bank and finance issues, brokers said. The SET index ended 9.98 points higher at 832.55.
Crude oil futures stayed weak in Singapore. March Brent was last traded 24 cents down at $22.83.
Hong Kong gold ended at US$355.00/50 an ounce against New York's US$354.10/60 close on Thursday.
The dollar hit a new 30-month high of 1.6038 against the mark and was steady against the yen in Europe. At 1035 GMT, the dollar was at 116.92/7.02 yen and 1.6037/42 marks.
